title: Correct without shaming
hookLine: from Alexander the grammarian: correct people's mistakes by saying the right thing yourself (Meditations 1.10)

lines: YOU WENT? WHAT DID YOU SEE?
cards: A four-year-old announces, I goed to the park. You have choices. You can say, no, it's went, say it again.
Or you can say, you went to the park? What did you see? Most parents learn, sooner or later, that the second way works better, and nobody cries.
Nearly two thousand years ago, a teacher of Greek grammar did the same with grown men, including a future emperor, and Marcus thought it worth a whole entry.

teach.b: First, the teacher. Alexander was a grammarian, a professional teacher of Greek language and literature, a respected job in Rome, and he taught the young Marcus.

A grammarian's whole life is noticing mistakes. Second, what he didn't do. Marcus says he learned from Alexander not to find fault, and not to jump on people who used a clumsy word, a wrong form or an odd-sounding phrase.
No pouncing. No public correction. Third, what he did instead.

teach.h: SLIP THE RIGHT WORD IN YOURSELF.
teach.b: He would slip the right expression into the conversation himself, neatly: as part of his answer, or while agreeing with the person, or while talking with them about the real subject, the thing itself, not the word.
The other person heard the right form, and nobody had been made small. Fourth, why it works.

teach.h: KEEP TO THE THING, NOT THE SLIP.
teach.b: Corrected in front of others, people usually hear one thing: that they were wrong in public. The lesson vanishes under the embarrassment.

Said right, in passing, the lesson arrives without the sting, and they can pick it up, or not. And notice Alexander's priority: the conversation stays on the subject, not the slip. This reaches past grammar.
A friend mispronounces a name. A colleague gets a fact slightly wrong in a meeting. A parent uses an old word for something.
Often the kindest correction is just the right word, said gently, in the next sentence. Marcus, who would one day have the power to humiliate anyone, wrote down a teacher who refused to.

how: Many parents, teachers and colleagues practice something like Alexander's way: they repeat the correct word or fact naturally in their reply instead of pointing out the mistake.

o: a strict teacher who made pupils repeat every error
the Macedonian king who conquered an empire to India
the grammarian who corrected mistakes without shaming

games.q: correct without shaming — tap the pairs.

s: Alexander corrected Marcus's grammar sharply in front of others
he avoided fault-finding and slipped the right form into his own reply.
Alexander kept talking about the real subject, not the word
the point of talking was the thing itself.
he made sure the right expression was heard, just gently.

games.q: in a meeting, a colleague mispronounces a client's name. what would Alexander the grammarian do?
o: correct them right away, in front of everyone.
never mention it, and never say the name either.
say the name correctly in your next sentence, and stay on the subject.
games.why: he introduced the right expression himself, by way of answer or agreement, and kept to the matter at hand.

practice: Remember a time someone corrected you in front of others, and feel how it landed, even now.

Then replay a time you did it to someone else, without judging it, but this time just use the right word yourself, in passing, and keep talking about the real subject. Watch their face in this version.

wordCard.voice: Alexander. The grammarian who never pounced on a mistake, saying the right thing himself, in passing, and keeping to the subject. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a grammarian, a teacher of language and literature, like Alexander.

carryVoice: Your line: say it right, gently. Keep to the thing, not the slip. Day five hundred twenty-seven, done.
